title: Read a declaration one scope at a time
objective: Follow values through a short declaration, an assignment and a shadowed name without running the program.
introduction: A useful way to read Go is to ask three questions at each assignment: which block owns this name, what type does it have, and is a new variable being created? The spelling of a name alone does not answer any of them.

sections.title: Trace the original variable
sections.body: Start with a local variable. Its type comes from the expression on the right. An ordinary assignment updates that same variable; it does not create another binding. Read the two lines as a small state table: first count is 2, then count is 5.
sections.code:
count := 2
count = count + 3
fmt.Println(count) // 5
sections.walkthrough: The right side is evaluated before the assignment. The old count contributes 2, the expression becomes 5, and only then is count updated. This is useful when stepping through a counter, an index or a retry budget.

sections.title: A nested block owns a different name
sections.body: An if body is a new lexical block. A short declaration there may hide an outer variable. This can be intentional for a temporary result, but it becomes confusing when the outer result was supposed to change.
sections.walkthrough: The inner name stops being accessible at the closing brace. Replacing its := with = would instead update the outer string. The difference is scope, not a special rule about if.

sections.title: Use the rule while reviewing real code
sections.body: In a multi-name short declaration, at least one non-blank name must be new in the same block. Existing names in that block keep their declared types. Before changing := to =, find every declaration and branch exit; an inner err may be a deliberate short-lived error, or it may hide the value returned later.

takeaway: Read the block before the operator. Prefer a short temporary scope when it clarifies ownership; use assignment when an existing result must change.
reviewAnswer: May hide an outer variable with a new local name
question: Which statement is correct about nested :=?
wrongAnswers: It is automatically overwritten when the block ends
It becomes a pointer to the inner variable
hint: Track each name together with the block that declares it.
nuance: A nested declaration and an assignment have different effects even when the name is spelled identically.

title: Read the failure path before the happy path
objective: Trace a result and error through a complete boundary, including wrapping and partial results.
introduction: An error result is part of a function contract. The caller needs to know whether a value is valid when err is non-nil, who should add context, and which layer decides what the user sees. A short early return makes that contract visible.

sections.title: Trace both returns
sections.body: This function promises a useful positive integer only when its error is nil. Invalid syntax and a non-positive number are different failures. In each failure branch, return immediately; the normal result appears once at the bottom.
sections.walkthrough: For "abc", Atoi fails and the first branch exits. For "0", parsing succeeds and validation fails. For "8", neither error branch runs and the caller receives 8, nil. No exception handler is needed to follow those paths.

sections.title: Handle it at the boundary
sections.body: The helper adds operation context without choosing an HTTP status or printing to a console. A CLI handler or HTTP adapter can decide how to report the error. Avoid logging the same error at every layer; repeated messages obscure a single failure.

sections.title: Partial results need a documented contract
sections.body: Some APIs deliberately return useful data with an error. io.Reader is a notable example: process the bytes returned before deciding what the error means. Do not generalize the early-return pattern into discarding all non-zero results. Read the particular API contract and distinguish expected absence, invalid input and infrastructure failure.

takeaway: Follow each return as a pair. Handle errors deliberately, preserve a useful cause with wrapping, and use partial values only when the API promises them.
reviewAnswer: Use partial data only when its API contract permits it
question: Which statement is correct about a result with an error?
wrongAnswers: Whenever the value is not its zero value
Only after converting the error to a string
hint: Walk through one invalid input and one valid input before reading the success return.
nuance: An error does not universally invalidate every returned value; the called API defines that contract.

title: A slice is a window, not a copied array
objective: Predict a subslice, an element write and append by tracking the backing array.
introduction: A slice describes a region of an array. Copying a slice value copies its descriptor, not all the elements. Two descriptors may therefore refer to the same elements while having different lengths and capacities.

sections.title: Draw the shared storage
sections.body: Treat the array as three numbered cells and each slice as a window over those cells. b begins at the second cell of a. Updating b[0] changes that cell; a observes it because it still refers to the same array.
sections.walkthrough: No goroutines are involved here. This is aliasing in a single execution flow. It matters for helper functions that appear to return a fresh view but actually let their callers change the original data.

sections.title: Capacity affects append, not ownership
sections.body: Append may reuse storage when capacity is available, or allocate storage when it is not. Assign its result because the returned descriptor can change. A full slice expression can restrict capacity, preventing an append through that view from using the hidden tail; existing element writes still share storage.
sections.walkthrough: This append must grow beyond b's capacity. Do not depend on a particular capacity growth factor; the language does not promise one.

sections.title: Choose a copy at the ownership boundary
sections.body: Use slices.Clone for an independent shallow copy of the elements. For slices of pointers or nested slices, the pointed-to objects remain shared. Decide whether you need a view, a shallow clone, or a domain-specific deep copy. Write that decision into the function contract instead of leaving callers to guess.

takeaway: Track array identity as well as len and cap. A different slice value can still expose the same mutable storage.
reviewAnswer: Can still share the original backing array
question: Which statement is correct about copying a slice header?
wrongAnswers: All elements into a new independent array
The original array and every object reachable from it
hint: Draw the array once and point both slice windows at it.
nuance: Capacity clipping controls append reuse; it does not isolate writes to elements already in the slice.

title: Shared slices and concurrent append
objective: Separate shared headers, shared elements and safe collection of concurrent results.
introduction: A goroutine does not make its arguments private. If two workers share a slice, you must reason about the slice descriptor and the array it refers to. Making extra goroutines can expose an ownership mistake that a sequential example concealed.

sections.title: Why append needs coordination
sections.body: Concurrent append to one shared slice variable reads and writes the same descriptor and may write the same backing storage. Even if capacity is large enough, append still changes the shared length. Reserving capacity is a performance choice, not synchronization.
sections.code:
// Unsafe: both goroutines update the same slice.
var results []int
go func() { results = append(results, 1) }()
go func() { results = append(results, 2) }()
sections.walkthrough: The outcome is not a reliable permutation of [1 2]. This is a deliberate counterexample, not code to copy. A passing test without the race detector does not establish safety.

sections.title: Give each worker a separate slot
sections.body: A pre-sized slice permits independent element writes when each worker owns a different index, no worker changes the descriptor, and the reader waits for every writer. Elements that themselves contain shared pointers need their own ownership rules.
sections.walkthrough: Index i is assigned to exactly one goroutine. WaitGroup orders the final read after the completed writes. For very large inputs, combine this ownership pattern with a bounded worker pool rather than starting a goroutine per item.

sections.title: Use a single collector for variable-length output
sections.body: If each job returns an unknown number of values, let workers send results to one owner that appends, or protect every access with the same mutex. A channel transfers values; it does not deep-copy a slice payload. The sender must stop mutating transferred storage or clone it first. Run race-enabled tests on a supported desktop toolchain; the app does not offer a native race detector.

takeaway: Concurrency safety comes from ownership and synchronization, not spare capacity. Distinct indexes plus a final join differ from concurrent append.
reviewAnswer: Needs one owner or synchronization, even with capacity
question: Which statement is correct about concurrent append?
wrongAnswers: Yes, allocation is the only shared operation
Yes, if the slice contains integers
hint: Separate the slice header from its elements and identify every writer.
nuance: Independent slots are safe only with fixed ownership and synchronization before the final read.

title: A tiny slice can keep a large buffer alive
objective: Recognize retained backing arrays and detach small long-lived results deliberately.
introduction: Visible length is not retained memory size. A small view can keep an entire allocation reachable. This is often noticed when a parser, cache or queue stores a few bytes from each large input and memory grows far beyond the stored lengths.

sections.title: Follow the reference that survives
sections.body: The function returns only sixteen bytes, but the result still points into the large allocation. As long as that backing array remains reachable, garbage collection cannot reclaim the array just because most of its bytes are outside the returned view.
sections.walkthrough: The 8 MiB allocation is an illustrative size, not a threshold in Go. The problem is the lifetime mismatch: a short prefix outlives the large buffer it views.

sections.title: Detach only what must outlive the input
sections.body: Copy a small result when it needs an independent lifetime. The copy costs time and an allocation, so use it at a boundary such as inserting into a long-lived cache, not indiscriminately inside every short-lived operation.
sections.walkthrough: Clipping capacity with data[:n:n] alone would not detach the original array. Setting one local variable to nil also does not help while another live view still refers to the allocation.

sections.title: Measure retention rather than guessing
sections.body: Distinguish bytes allocated over time from bytes still live. A temporary copy can increase allocation traffic while reducing retained memory. Inspect heap profiles in the real service, reproduce with representative payloads, and compare before and after. For slices of pointers, discarded elements can also retain pointed-to objects; use appropriate clearing or slices helpers when shrinking reusable storage.

takeaway: Optimize lifetimes, not just lengths. A small copy can release a much larger backing array once all other references are gone.
reviewAnswer: Can retain a much larger backing allocation
question: Which statement is correct about a long-lived subslice?
wrongAnswers: Clipping capacity with data[:n:n]
Assigning a second variable to the same slice
hint: Look for a small cached value that still points into a large input.
nuance: Reducing a slice capacity does not copy storage or shorten the backing array lifetime.

title: More goroutines are not more capacity
objective: Bound active workers and queued work according to the resource that actually limits throughput.
introduction: Concurrency is how work overlaps. Capacity is how much useful work the system can sustain. A thousand waiting goroutines do not give Redis a thousand extra cores or increase a database connection budget. They do consume memory, queue time and cancellation bookkeeping.

sections.title: Start with a budget
sections.body: Suppose one downstream operation takes about 20 ms at the target load. Twenty concurrent operations can support roughly 1,000 operations per second in that simplified steady-state example. Real latency distributions, payload size and server limits change the result. Treat it as a sizing hypothesis, then measure tail latency and saturation.

sections.title: Apply admission control before creating more work
sections.body: A fixed worker count bounds active calls. A bounded jobs channel also bounds queued work. A context-aware producer stops waiting when the request is no longer useful. This fragment shows the admission point; workers, cancellation and channel ownership must all belong to the same enclosing operation.
sections.walkthrough: Do not launch a new goroutine for every rejected or blocked enqueue: that merely moves an unbounded queue from the channel into goroutine stacks.

sections.title: Pick a deliberate overload response
sections.body: For request/response traffic, reject work that cannot meet its deadline or wait only within a bounded budget. For background work, use a durable queue if losing work is unacceptable. A worker pool limits concurrency, not requests per second; add rate limiting when the downstream contract is a rate. Track active calls, queue depth, queue age, errors and latency together.

takeaway: Bound workers, waiting work and waiting time. Size those limits from downstream behavior, then verify under load.
reviewAnswer: Limits concurrent jobs, not requests per second
question: Which statement is correct about a bounded worker pool?
wrongAnswers: It increases the dependency's physical capacity automatically
It removes all queueing and timeout costs
hint: Find the slowest resource and the queue in front of it.
nuance: An unbounded population of goroutines waiting for a semaphore is still an unbounded queue.

title: Cancellation is a request; joining proves exit
objective: Design a worker so it can stop waiting and its owner can wait for it to finish.
introduction: Starting a goroutine creates an obligation: identify who asks it to stop and who observes that it has stopped. Canceling a context closes a signal; it does not terminate arbitrary Go code. Every blocking point must cooperate or have another bounded exit.

sections.title: A blocked send needs an escape
sections.body: A producer may outlive its consumer. If the consumer returns early, an unconditional send can wait forever and keep its goroutine and reachable objects alive. Select between sending and cancellation.
sections.walkthrough: If the send and cancellation are both ready, select may choose either. Design the protocol to tolerate that race in intent; cancellation does not mean no operation can ever finish afterwards.

sections.title: Wait for the owned goroutine
sections.body: A done channel acknowledges exit. The owner cancels, then waits. The worker must observe ctx, including inside downstream operations, or this wait can still block. Production shutdown also needs an overall timeout and a clear policy when a dependency refuses to return.
sections.walkthrough: The worker closes done because it owns the completion signal. Do not close a work channel from an unrelated receiver while senders may still use it.

sections.title: Use a lifecycle checklist
sections.body: For every worker, list start, inputs, outputs, stop signal and join point. Include error paths, not only success. Context does not interrupt a mutex lock or CPU loop automatically; choose primitives and loop checkpoints accordingly. A finalizer or the garbage collector is not a goroutine cleanup strategy.

takeaway: Cancellation communicates intent. A join or completion acknowledgement establishes that the owned work has actually stopped.
reviewAnswer: Request a stop, then observe the worker finishing
question: Which statement is correct about cancellation and joining?
wrongAnswers: Every goroutine using it has already exited
Every blocking primitive is forcibly interrupted
hint: Identify the stop signal and the acknowledgement as two separate events.
nuance: A context only helps at code paths and APIs that observe it; cancellation alone does not join workers.

title: Stacks, escape analysis and object lifetimes
objective: Explain why returning a local address is safe and why allocation placement must be measured.
introduction: Lifetime is the semantic question: how long must a value remain usable? Stack and heap placement are implementation choices used to satisfy that requirement. The compiler performs escape analysis; source syntax alone is not a dependable allocation profiler.

sections.title: A local address can safely leave a function
sections.body: Returning a pointer to a local value is normal Go. The implementation arranges storage so callers do not receive a dangling pointer. Do not import C stack-lifetime rules into this code.
sections.walkthrough: The local spelling c does not disappear in a way that invalidates the returned pointer. Exactly which allocations survive optimization can depend on inlining and the surrounding call sites.

sections.title: Pointers are a design decision first
sections.body: A value receiver copies its receiver; a pointer receiver allows shared mutation and may be required by method sets. Neither form is universally faster. Large copies, escaping references, cache locality and synchronization all matter. Start with ownership and API semantics, then inspect a benchmark that represents the actual use.

sections.title: Inspect the native build, not an assumption
sections.body: On a desktop Go installation, compiler diagnostics can report escape decisions. Their wording and decisions can change across versions; they are observations, not API guarantees.
sections.code:
go build -gcflags="-m=2" ./...
go test -bench=. -benchmem ./...
sections.walkthrough: Use these commands in your development environment. Compare allocations per operation and time after warm-up. The app's WebAssembly sandbox does not reproduce every native service allocation or threading cost.

takeaway: Reason about required lifetime first. Use compiler diagnostics and measurements to learn how the implementation realizes it.
reviewAnswer: Helps determine stack versus heap storage
question: Which statement is correct about escape analysis?
wrongAnswers: The pointer always expires on the next function call
The caller must manually free the local stack frame
hint: Separate the language lifetime guarantee from a particular allocation decision.
nuance: Pointer syntax does not prove a heap allocation, and a value expression is not a promise of zero allocations.

title: What the garbage collector can and cannot free
objective: Follow references from roots and distinguish unreachable objects from unwanted live data.
introduction: Garbage collection reclaims memory that the runtime determines is no longer reachable. It does not know that an application has lost interest in a cache entry, nor does it close a forgotten network connection on a useful schedule. Ownership still matters.

sections.title: Think in reference paths
sections.body: Imagine a global cache holding a pointer to an order, which points to a large receipt buffer. As long as a live reference path reaches the buffer, it is not garbage. Removing one local reference is insufficient when the cache still holds another.
sections.walkthrough: Delete removes this map entry, not every possible reference to the order. Concurrent access to the map would require synchronization. The example focuses only on the reference graph.

sections.title: Collection is not immediate destruction
sections.body: An unreachable allocation becomes eligible for reclamation; there is no promise that the operating system immediately receives the same amount of memory. Runtime-managed free space can be reused. RSS, live heap and total allocated bytes answer different questions, so compare like with like when diagnosing growth.

sections.title: Resources need explicit lifetime management
sections.body: Close files and response bodies, stop owned background workers, and bound caches according to their contracts. A tracing collector can collect unreachable cycles, but it cannot make an indefinitely blocked goroutine release the values it still reaches. Avoid finalizers as normal cleanup: their timing does not establish a reliable resource protocol.

takeaway: The GC answers reachability, not business usefulness. Remove unwanted references and close resources explicitly; then measure the correct memory metric.
reviewAnswer: Stays live until its remaining references disappear
question: Which statement is correct about a cached reachable object?
wrongAnswers: The garbage collector never handles byte slices
Setting any variable to nil disables future collection
hint: Follow every remaining reference path, including caches and blocked workers.
nuance: Eligible for collection does not mean the same bytes disappear from process RSS immediately.

title: GC cost, allocation rate and memory budgets
objective: Distinguish reducing live data from tuning collection frequency and respect a container memory limit.
introduction: A service pays for memory in more than one way: live objects occupy space, new allocations create work, and collection uses CPU. Tuning a single GC knob cannot repair an unbounded cache or a queue that retains every request body.

sections.title: Measure two different problems
sections.body: A high allocation rate with a small live heap suggests churn: many objects become garbage quickly. A growing live heap suggests retained data or a growing workload. Capture representative profiles before changing code; removing one temporary allocation is not helpful if a cache retains gigabytes indefinitely.

sections.title: Treat settings as tradeoffs
sections.body: GOGC influences the heap-growth target and therefore the tradeoff between collection frequency and memory. GOMEMLIMIT is a soft runtime memory limit, not an operating-system hard cap. Native allocations and other process memory can require additional budget. Leave measured headroom under the container limit rather than making the two numbers equal.
sections.code:
# Illustrative native-service configuration, not an iOS setting:
GOGC=100 GOMEMLIMIT=400MiB ./service
sections.walkthrough: The 400 MiB value is an example, not a recommendation for every 512 MiB container. Measure your binary, traffic and non-runtime memory before choosing a value.

sections.title: Reduce work before aggressive tuning
sections.body: Avoid retaining whole request graphs in queues, bound cache entries, and reuse buffers only with clear ownership and size limits. Increasing a memory allowance may reduce collection frequency but raises memory use; forcing very frequent GC can waste CPU. A pool is an optimization with lifecycle constraints, not a guarantee that objects will stay cached or that memory use is bounded.

takeaway: First bound live data and measure allocation churn. Then tune collection within an observed process budget and recheck latency under load.
reviewAnswer: A soft runtime budget, not a process hard cap
question: Which statement is correct about gomemlimit?
wrongAnswers: Yes, it caps every byte used by the process
Yes, it also bounds caches and request queues
hint: Compare allocation rate, live heap and process memory before choosing a knob.
nuance: The runtime memory limit is soft and cannot substitute for a bounded workload or a measured container budget.

title: Goroutines, OS threads and GOMAXPROCS
objective: Explain concurrency versus parallel execution without assuming a goroutine is an OS thread.
introduction: A goroutine is a Go execution task scheduled by the runtime. An OS thread is an operating-system execution resource. The runtime multiplexes tasks onto threads; counting goroutines therefore does not tell you how many cores are doing useful work.

sections.title: Use the G, M, P model carefully
sections.body: In runtime terminology G represents a goroutine, M an OS thread, and P the scheduler resources needed to execute ordinary Go code. GOMAXPROCS controls how many Ps execute Go code at once. It is not a limit on total goroutines or a universal limit on all process threads.

sections.title: CPU work and waiting behave differently
sections.body: Several CPU-bound tasks need available execution capacity to run in parallel. Waiting network operations can overlap while other work proceeds. Starting ten thousand CPU-heavy goroutines does not create ten thousand cores and may add scheduling overhead. Native defaults can account for runtime and container configuration; inspect the actual service instead of copying a magic setting.
sections.code:
fmt.Println("Go execution slots:", runtime.GOMAXPROCS(0))
fmt.Println("goroutines now:", runtime.NumGoroutine())
sections.walkthrough: Passing zero queries the current GOMAXPROCS value. NumGoroutine is a snapshot and includes runtime/application work; it is a diagnostic signal, not a precise request counter.

sections.title: Choose the right concurrency level
sections.body: For CPU work, benchmark a bounded pool around the available CPU budget. For I/O work, use downstream concurrency, queue and deadline limits. A service can be overloaded with many waiting tasks even when CPU looks low. The iOS app's WebAssembly execution environment does not demonstrate native OS-thread behavior; these examples describe native Go services.

takeaway: Goroutines express concurrency. The runtime and OS determine parallel execution within available CPU and downstream budgets.
reviewAnswer: Limits parallel Go execution slots, not goroutines
question: Which statement is correct about gomaxprocs?
wrongAnswers: Yes, each goroutine reserves a physical core
Yes, once the goroutine has a large enough stack
hint: Count tasks, execution slots and operating-system threads as different quantities.
nuance: A low CPU percentage can coexist with severe overload caused by blocked downstream calls and growing queues.

title: Find a leak by following evidence
objective: Choose a heap profile, goroutine profile, CPU profile or trace to test a specific hypothesis.
introduction: A rising memory graph is a symptom. Before changing code, ask whether traffic grew, objects are retained, workers are stuck, or allocation churn became expensive. Different diagnostic tools answer different questions.

sections.title: Choose the observation
sections.body: A heap profile helps find retained allocations; allocation profiles emphasize cumulative allocation traffic. A goroutine profile shows where tasks wait. CPU sampling identifies code consuming CPU, while an execution trace exposes scheduling and blocking relationships. Compare the same workload and interval rather than comparing unrelated snapshots.

sections.title: Write a bounded diagnostic capture
sections.body: For a native local program, a goroutine profile can be written to a file without opening an HTTP diagnostics server. Handle the file error and close the file. Profiles can include operational details, so store and share them deliberately.
sections.walkthrough: This fragment belongs inside an error-returning diagnostic function and imports os and runtime/pprof. Capture once at the relevant time; do not create an unbounded stream of profile files.

sections.title: Turn a suspicion into a comparison
sections.body: If goroutine count grows after requests finish, compare stacks and identify the owner of the repeated wait. If heap grows with cache keys, inspect eviction and reference lifetimes. Change one thing and repeat the workload. A single stable run does not prove absence of races or leaks, and profiling overhead itself should be considered.

takeaway: Name the hypothesis, choose a tool that can observe it, and compare equivalent workloads before and after the change.
reviewAnswer: Shows stacks that help locate blocked workers
question: Which statement is correct about a goroutine profile?
wrongAnswers: Only the application binary size
Only the total number of source files
hint: Pick the profile that can actually observe the suspected resource.
nuance: Profiles need workload context; a large cumulative allocation total does not itself establish a live-memory leak.

title: An HTTP request has a lifecycle and a budget
objective: Separate request parsing, domain work, downstream deadlines and response writing.
introduction: A Go web service is more than a route callback. Every request consumes a connection, parsing work, application time and possibly downstream capacity. Give those resources explicit lifetimes. This lesson describes native server code; guest Go programs in the app cannot open network sockets.

sections.title: Keep the boundary small
sections.body: A handler translates a protocol into an application operation: validate input, call a service with the request context, then map the result to a response. Domain logic should not need a ResponseWriter. If the client leaves, the request context can notify cooperative downstream work.

sections.title: Configure a server rather than only a callback
sections.body: This is a native-server configuration fragment. Header and idle timeouts address specific connection phases; they are not a complete business-operation deadline. WriteTimeout must fit the response type, especially streaming, rather than being copied blindly.
sections.walkthrough: The values are illustrative. Add request-body limits, operation-specific deadlines and response policies based on the API. A timeout does not undo an operation the remote service already committed.

sections.title: Choose HTTP when it matches the problem
sections.body: HTTP APIs fit request/response interactions and interoperability. A batch program or local library may need no server at all. Test handlers with httptest and in-memory requests before deployment. In-memory handler tests check application behavior; they do not prove production TLS, socket, proxy or load-balancer configuration.

takeaway: A handler is an adapter with explicit resource limits. Pass context into the application and test protocol behavior without requiring a running network service.
reviewAnswer: Translates requests and responses around a use case
question: Which statement is correct about an http adapter?
wrongAnswers: Owning every domain rule and database implementation
Guaranteeing a remote operation is undone after timeout
hint: Follow the request from validation to the final response, including cancellation.
nuance: Connection-phase timeouts and a business operation deadline protect different parts of a request.

title: Gin routes are adapters, not the whole application
objective: Read route groups, path parameters and injected dependencies in a small Gin API.
introduction: Gin supplies routing, middleware and request/response helpers on top of net/http. It is useful when those conventions reduce repeated adapter code. It does not supply your domain model, persistence policy or downstream capacity, and a small API can also use the standard library.

sections.title: Read the route from left to right
sections.body: New creates an engine without the default middleware set. The group applies a common path prefix. A named segment is read from the Gin context, then handed to a service. This is an illustrative fragment: store and its result/error contract are application dependencies.
sections.walkthrough: This simplified example treats Find failure uniformly. A real adapter should distinguish not-found from timeout, cancellation and internal failure rather than returning 404 for all of them.

sections.title: Inject the dependency, not a global registry
sections.body: Construct a handler with the interface it needs, then register methods on the engine. That makes a fake store available to tests and avoids hiding process configuration in globals. Keep route names and response shapes stable as an external contract.

sections.title: Test routing without starting a server
sections.body: A Gin engine implements http.Handler, so httptest can send an in-memory request through the router and middleware. Assert status, headers and body, including errors. The app includes local-preview patterns, but these reading examples are not a promise that every Gin version or native networking feature runs in its sandbox.

takeaway: Use Gin to express the HTTP adapter. Keep application behavior behind explicit dependencies and test the adapter through its Handler interface.
reviewAnswer: Shares a URL prefix and middleware between routes
question: Which statement is correct about a gin route group?
wrongAnswers: It creates a separate operating-system process for every route
It automatically implements the database layer
hint: Read the path prefix, route pattern, parameter and response in that order.
nuance: Gin is optional tooling around HTTP; it does not make an application architecture or network policy for you.

title: Validate a request before doing side effects
objective: Follow JSON binding, size limits, validation and a safe error response.
introduction: Decoded JSON is not yet trusted application input. A field can have the right Go type and still violate a business rule. Bound the body, handle decoding failure, then apply domain validation before writing to storage or calling another service.

sections.title: Separate decoding from application rules
sections.body: This adapter accepts a JSON object with a non-empty name. ShouldBindJSON lets the handler choose its error response instead of relying on an automatically written status. The body cap is a policy example and should match the endpoint.
sections.walkthrough: The generic error avoids echoing an arbitrary decoder message. A production API can map an over-limit body to 413 and expose structured, documented field errors. Decide whether unknown JSON fields should be rejected and configure that policy deliberately.

sections.title: Validation does not provide authorization
sections.body: A valid item ID does not prove the requester may access that item. Authenticate the caller, check authorization at the relevant boundary, and keep secrets out of logs and responses. Binding tags check specified shapes; business invariants may require several fields and current state.

sections.title: Test the cases users actually send
sections.body: Cover missing fields, wrong types, malformed and oversized input, duplicate requests and unexpected fields according to the chosen policy. Specify whether optional zero values differ from missing values. If accepting a command has an external effect, consider an idempotency contract rather than assuming retries are harmless.

takeaway: Decode, validate shape, enforce business rules and authorization, then perform side effects. Each step has a different responsibility.
reviewAnswer: Does not prove authorization or every business rule
question: Which statement is correct about successful json binding?
wrongAnswers: The user is authorized to access every referenced record
The request is safe to retry after any side effect
hint: Find the point where input first becomes allowed to cause a side effect.
nuance: Required fields and authorization are different checks; valid JSON can still represent an invalid operation.

title: Redis is fast; its capacity is still finite
objective: Distinguish client pool limits, request deadlines, rate limits and bounded command batches.
introduction: Redis can be overwhelmed by too much work, large payloads, expensive commands or many clients competing for the same resources. Making every slice element a goroutine only moves pressure downstream. Treat the server, the network and the client pool as separate budgets.

sections.title: Understand what a client pool limits
sections.body: A shared client normally reuses connections. Creating a new client for each request defeats that reuse. A connection-pool setting is not automatically a global rate limiter, and waiting for a connection still consumes request time. Exact option semantics depend on the client version; read its production documentation.

sections.title: Give each operation a bounded lifetime
sections.body: This native Go fragment assumes a configured shared go-redis client. Missing keys and infrastructure failures are different cases. The request context carries the parent lifetime; the shorter local timeout bounds this particular operation.
sections.walkthrough: 150 ms is an example, not a universal Redis timeout. Configure and verify client network timeouts as well; do not assume a context deadline replaces every transport setting.

sections.title: Batch for efficiency without removing limits
sections.body: Pipelining can reduce network round trips, but an enormous pipeline can increase queued work and memory. Bound batch size and total payload, avoid broad scans or expensive hot-path commands, and monitor server latency, errors, pool waits and command volume. Test fallback behavior too: when the cache slows, a sudden flood of misses can overload the database behind it.

takeaway: Limit work before it reaches Redis. A pool, timeout, rate limiter and bounded pipeline solve different parts of the capacity problem.
reviewAnswer: Reuses connections; it is not a request-rate limit
question: Which statement is correct about a redis connection pool?
wrongAnswers: Yes, every connection always allows exactly one request per second
Yes, it also bounds every other application instance
hint: Identify the client pool, the queue and the server as separate limits.
nuance: A cache outage can become a database outage if fallback traffic has no admission control.

title: Cache misses, retries and overload amplification
objective: Design a cache-miss path that avoids multiplying identical work and ambiguous retries.
introduction: A cache is often added to reduce load, yet its failure path can multiply load. When a popular key expires, many callers may fetch the same value at once. When a timeout triggers retries at several layers, one user action can become many downstream operations.

sections.title: Collapse duplicate work within a process
sections.body: singleflight lets concurrent callers for the same key share one in-flight computation. The loader should have an explicit bounded lifetime. In this fragment loadCtx is owned by the service, not borrowed indefinitely from whichever request happened to arrive first.
sections.walkthrough: group is a shared singleflight.Group. This synchronous form waits for the shared result; callers that must independently stop waiting need a cancellation-aware design, for example DoChan with a select. Coalescing is per process, not a distributed lock across replicas.

sections.title: Define cache freshness and failure policy
sections.body: Choose TTLs from the data contract. Jitter can spread expirations, but it does not make stale data acceptable automatically. Serving a stale value may be useful for a catalogue and wrong for an authorization decision. Bound key count and value size, and ensure a miss cannot start unlimited fallback work.

sections.title: Retry only a retryable, safe operation
sections.body: Use a small attempt budget, backoff with jitter and an overall deadline. A timed-out write may already have committed, so an automatic retry can duplicate a side effect without an idempotency contract. Coordinate retries at one layer where possible. Record attempts and final outcomes so apparent success does not conceal amplified downstream load.

takeaway: Coalesce duplicates, bound fallback work and retry under an explicit contract. A faster happy path does not excuse an unbounded failure path.
reviewAnswer: Coalesces in-flight work per key within one process
question: Which statement is correct about singleflight.group?
wrongAnswers: All replicas and all Redis clients worldwide
Every completed request forever, like a persistent cache
hint: Follow one expired hot key through every replica and retry layer.
nuance: An in-flight duplicate suppressor is neither a persistent cache nor a distributed lock.

title: Packages follow responsibilities, not a diagram
objective: Choose cohesive package boundaries and keep concrete dependencies at the edges.
introduction: Go packages provide namespaces and compile-time dependency boundaries. More packages do not automatically create a cleaner design. Start with behavior that changes together, then separate a boundary when it hides an implementation detail or makes a dependency direction clearer.

sections.title: Keep names useful at the call site
sections.body: A package named orders can expose orders.Service or orders.Create without repeating a business prefix everywhere. A package called utils tends to accumulate unrelated dependencies because its purpose does not constrain what belongs there. Prefer a name that explains why its exported operations belong together.

sections.title: Let the consumer name a small interface
sections.body: The application needs the operation Save, not every method of the database client. Define that need near the code that uses it, and inject an implementation when wiring the process.
sections.walkthrough: The concrete SQL or Redis adapter can satisfy this interface implicitly. Do not create an interface for every struct by habit; add it where substitution or a stable boundary is useful.

sections.title: Review dependency direction
sections.body: HTTP handlers can depend on application operations; those operations should not need a router context. Keep protocol and storage types from spreading through every function. An internal directory can restrict which importers may use a package, but it does not make a design cohesive by itself. Watch for import cycles as a signal that responsibilities may be entangled.

sections.title: Draw an import graph before a folder tree
sections.body: Start from changes the team makes together: placing an order, pricing it and persisting it. A package should expose the vocabulary needed by its callers, not its database layout. Put transport decoding in an adapter and business decisions behind a narrow application API. Draw arrows for actual Go imports: a cycle means responsibilities must move or a smaller contract must be introduced. Renaming directories to domain, service and repository does not remove coupling if every package imports one shared mutable model.
sections.code:
cmd/shop/main.go
internal/orders/service.go
internal/orders/order.go
internal/postgres/orders.go
internal/httpapi/orders.go
sections.walkthrough: This is a focused layout or boundary fragment, not a second standalone program. Read it together with the complete worked example above.

sections.title: Use internal without promising more than it enforces
sections.body: The internal directory limits which importers may use a package; it does not make methods or data private between sibling packages. Unexport identifiers that clients do not need. Keep reusable libraries outside internal only when they have real independent consumers and a compatibility policy. Avoid a util package that accumulates unrelated helpers: move a helper beside its consumer until two callers reveal one coherent abstraction. Package boundaries and module version boundaries solve different problems.

sections.title: Check a boundary with a change experiment
sections.body: Imagine replacing Postgres with a fake for a service test. If the service imports SQL row types, the dependency crosses the intended boundary. Then imagine adding one order rule: it should be tested without HTTP. Finally inspect exported names with go doc and examine direct dependencies with go list. A good boundary makes these changes local; it does not require a dedicated interface and a separate file for every type. Record the ownership rule in package documentation so the next feature can preserve it.

takeaway: A good boundary reduces what a caller must know. Use cohesive packages and small consumer-owned contracts where they remove real coupling.
reviewAnswer: Names the behavior its caller needs from a dependency
question: Which statement is correct about a consumer-owned interface?
wrongAnswers: In a universal package containing every database API
As a mandatory duplicate for every concrete type
hint: Describe the caller's required behavior before naming the implementation.
nuance: A directory tree is not architecture unless dependencies and responsibilities actually follow its boundaries.

strengths: A package has one clear reason to change
Import direction can be reviewed and tested
cautions: A folder name does not enforce a boundary
Generic utils packages accumulate unrelated dependencies

title: Ports and adapters with a real request
objective: Trace an HTTP adapter through an application operation to a storage port and compare test boundaries.
introduction: Ports and adapters is a way to keep a use case independent of delivery and infrastructure details. It is useful when one behavior has several entry points or storage implementations. The value comes from dependency direction, not from the number of folders named domain.

sections.title: Trace one operation
sections.body: A request body becomes a CreateOrder command. The application validates business rules and calls an OrderStore port. The HTTP adapter translates the outcome back into protocol terms. The storage adapter translates the port operation into its own database protocol. Domain rules do not inspect HTTP headers or SQL row objects.

sections.title: Keep orchestration readable
sections.body: This example is an application fragment. Validation runs before persistence. The error receives operation context while the caller retains access to its cause.
sections.walkthrough: The interface does not define transaction semantics by magic. If creating an order and publishing an event must be atomic, design that consistency boundary explicitly, for example with a database transaction and an outbox.

sections.title: Test at more than one boundary
sections.body: A fake store can test the use case cheaply, but cannot prove that a SQL adapter writes the right schema. Add integration tests for adapters and a smaller number of end-to-end journeys. Keep fakes faithful to important failure contracts, including cancellation and duplicate requests. Avoid adding layers when a small program has no substitution or ownership problem to solve.

sections.title: Put the port beside the use case
sections.body: The application asks for a capability such as reserving inventory, not for a generic database connection. Define the smallest interface that the application consumes, with domain values and context.Context for work that can block. A SQL adapter implements that contract; a test fake implements the same observable behavior. The executable constructs the adapter and injects it into the use case. The port does not import HTTP, SQL drivers or framework types. One struct can implement several consumer-specific interfaces without declaring it explicitly.

sections.title: Map errors and transactions deliberately
sections.body: A repository adapter can translate sql.ErrNoRows into the application absence contract instead of leaking SQL details. An HTTP adapter maps that stable error category to a response and logs once. If a use case changes several records atomically, expose one transaction-scoped operation or unit-of-work boundary whose lifetime the use case controls. Calling three repository methods independently does not create a transaction. Keep a remote payment request outside a long database transaction and design reconciliation for a payment that succeeds before local persistence fails.

sections.title: Test the contract, not just the fake
sections.body: A fake that always returns success can hide wrong SQL behavior. Run a shared repository contract against both fake and real adapter: missing record, duplicate identifier, cancellation and commit failure matter. Use application tests for business rules and adapter tests for SQL mapping. The extra abstraction earns its place when rules outlive a transport or infrastructure choice; a small read-only command can call one concrete implementation directly and introduce a port later.

takeaway: Use a port to express an application need and an adapter to translate an external mechanism. Verify both the use case and the concrete boundary.
reviewAnswer: Expresses a use case need independently of the database
question: Which statement is correct about a storage port?
wrongAnswers: Every table and wire command used by all databases
An automatic transaction spanning unrelated external services
hint: Trace a single request rather than adding layers to an abstract diagram.
nuance: Mocking a dependency tests a contract in isolation; it does not verify the concrete adapter honors that contract.

flow: Application use case owns its ports
Driven adapter implements an external operation
strengths: The same use case has CLI, HTTP or test drivers
Policy should be tested without a database
cautions: Adapters still need real integration tests
A port per field creates unnecessary indirection

title: Choose a style; keep the code easy to change
objective: Compare a modular monolith, layered design and microservices using concrete operational tradeoffs.
introduction: Architecture is a choice about boundaries, change and failure. A modular monolith can keep strong internal boundaries with one deployment. Microservices can separate ownership and release schedules, but add remote calls, distributed failures, versioning and operational work.

sections.title: Choose the smallest useful distribution boundary
sections.body: A small team sharing one transaction model may benefit from one deployable process with cohesive packages. Separate services become useful when independent scaling, ownership or delivery outweighs coordination costs. A folder named services does not make a monolith distributed, and a network hop does not make a boundary clean.

sections.title: Make the normal path visible
sections.body: Early returns keep a short function focused on its successful operation. Names should explain domain meaning; return errors at the layer able to add useful context. Avoid a generic helper that hides the important policy decision from its caller.
sections.walkthrough: This fragment makes the ordering of policy checks explicit. The real operation still needs an atomicity and idempotency contract if reservation changes external state. Shorter code is not cleaner when it conceals those obligations.

sections.title: Use a change-oriented checklist
sections.body: Ask whether one business change requires edits across unrelated packages; whether error ownership is clear; whether interfaces have real consumers; and whether tests describe observable behavior instead of private function calls. Keep formatting with gofmt, document surprising contracts, and remove abstractions that do not pay for their indirection. No architecture style eliminates concurrency, capacity or consistency tradeoffs.

sections.title: Compare decisions on the same axis
sections.body: Monolith and microservices describe deployment and ownership boundaries. Layered, hexagonal, Clean and Onion describe responsibility and source dependencies. Vertical slices organize change around features; MVC organizes presentation. DDD is a modeling approach, CQRS separates write and read models, and event sourcing chooses a state history as authority. A modular monolith can use hexagonal ports, vertical slices and CQRS together. Record the quality goal before comparing scores.

sections.title: Separate three architecture questions
sections.body: First choose code organization: packages by capability, layers or vertical slices. Next choose state coordination: local transactions, asynchronous events or event history. Finally choose deployment topology: one executable, functions or independent services. These are different axes. A modular monolith can use hexagonal boundaries and CQRS; a microservice can still have tangled internal code. Describe the constraint a choice solves before comparing editorial ratings. Scores are scenario-specific recommendations, not performance measurements.

sections.title: Write an architecture decision with an exit condition
sections.body: A useful decision record contains the workload, team ownership, correctness requirements, candidate approaches, chosen tradeoff and what evidence would reopen the decision. For a small team, one deployable with local transactions may beat independently deployable services despite an ambitious diagram. Revisit when measured scaling, fault isolation or team release independence becomes a constraint. Do not migrate because a style receives a higher score in a different scenario.

sections.title: Make quality visible at the seams
sections.body: Review one request from input validation to durable effect and response. Who owns the transaction? Who retries? Where is authorization enforced? Which boundary receives a deadline, and which log identifies the operation without exposing credentials? Then inspect tests at these seams. Small functions alone cannot repair contradictory ownership or undefined failure recovery. Prefer the simplest architecture that makes the required guarantees testable and operationally understandable.

takeaway: Choose boundaries for real change and ownership needs. Clear names, explicit errors, narrow contracts and behavioral tests matter in every architecture style.
reviewAnswer: Keeps module boundaries in one deployable process
question: Which statement is correct about a modular monolith?
wrongAnswers: It must expose every internal operation over a network
It cannot have independent modules or tests
hint: Compare the cost of a boundary with the change it makes easier.
nuance: Distribution adds failure modes and operational work; it is not a prerequisite for clean Go code.

flow: State the quality goal and constraints
Compare ownership, consistency and deployment costs
Record a decision and a measurable revisit trigger
strengths: A team needs to explain why a style fits
Architecture should evolve with evidence
cautions: Ratings are editorial starting points, not benchmarks
DDD, CQRS and deployment styles describe different axes

title: Bash essentials: navigate, inspect and copy files
objective: Use pwd, cd, ls, mkdir, cp and mv in a small disposable workspace.
introduction: A shell starts in a working directory, and relative paths are resolved there. Before building or moving files, establish that location. These exercises use a new scratch directory on your own Mac or Linux machine; no administrator permissions are needed.

sections.title: Locate the project before changing it
sections.body: pwd prints the working directory; ls -la includes hidden entries and metadata. cd changes this shell, not every terminal. The home shortcut is expanded by the shell, while a quoted path can contain spaces.
sections.code:
pwd
ls -la
cd "$HOME"
pwd
sections.walkthrough: Compare the two pwd results. ls -la may show .git, but that alone does not establish a repository root. Quoting "$HOME" passes a single path, even if it contains spaces.

sections.title: Create and copy a small fixture
sections.body: mktemp -d makes a unique scratch directory. mkdir -p creates missing directory components. cp copies bytes; mv changes the path. Keep the original until you have inspected the destination rather than experimenting on project files.
sections.code:
scratch_dir=$(mktemp -d)
mkdir -p "$scratch_dir/input" "$scratch_dir/output"
printf "%s\n" "hello Go" > "$scratch_dir/input/note.txt"
cp "$scratch_dir/input/note.txt" "$scratch_dir/output/copy.txt"
mv "$scratch_dir/output/copy.txt" "$scratch_dir/output/result.txt"
cat "$scratch_dir/output/result.txt"
sections.walkthrough: The final line prints hello Go. The > operator creates or truncates the named file; it is appropriate here because the fixture is new. The scratch path stays in scratch_dir for the next command.

sections.title: Check the result and remove only the fixture
sections.body: wc -l counts newline-terminated lines, and cmp compares the copied content. rm removes the specifically named fixture files; rmdir removes only empty directories, making an unexpected leftover visible instead of recursively erasing it.
sections.code:
wc -l "$scratch_dir/output/result.txt"
cmp "$scratch_dir/input/note.txt" "$scratch_dir/output/result.txt"
rm "$scratch_dir/input/note.txt" "$scratch_dir/output/result.txt"
rmdir "$scratch_dir/input" "$scratch_dir/output" "$scratch_dir"
sections.walkthrough: wc should report one line. cmp is silent with status zero for identical files. The cleanup names only files this exercise created; rmdir fails if another file remains, so inspect rather than adding recursive deletion.

takeaway: Start by checking the working directory, quote paths, and verify copied bytes before removing anything. Practice filesystem changes in a named scratch workspace, not in your only project copy.
reviewAnswer: Prints the current working directory
question: What does pwd show?
wrongAnswers: Every file under your home directory
The path of the Go compiler executable
hint: Relative paths begin at the current working directory.
nuance: cd affects its own shell; another terminal can be in a different directory.

title: Find code and inspect logs from the command line
objective: Combine find, grep, head, tail, sort and uniq without hiding their exit behavior.
introduction: Most development investigations begin with a filename, a symbol or a short log fragment. Use small commands to narrow the evidence before opening a huge file. The examples assume you are in a trusted Go project and have a text application log named app.log.

sections.title: Find source files and search their content
sections.body: find selects filesystem entries; grep searches text. The quoted pattern *.go is passed to find rather than expanded by Bash. -exec passes each discovered filename as an argument, preserving spaces without parsing the output of ls.
sections.code:
find . -type f -name "*.go"
find . -type f -name "*.go" -exec grep -nH -F "ListenAndServe" {} +
sections.walkthrough: The first command lists Go files. The second prints filename, line number and matching text. No matches can produce a nonzero grep status; distinguish that normal search outcome from an unreadable file.

sections.title: Read a bounded part of a log
sections.body: head shows the beginning, tail the end, and tail -f follows appended data until Ctrl-C. Bound a first inspection instead of loading a multi-gigabyte file. Filtering stdout does not capture stderr from a program unless you redirect it explicitly.
sections.code:
head -n 10 app.log
tail -n 40 app.log
grep -n -F "timeout" app.log
tail -f app.log
sections.walkthrough: Stop tail -f with Ctrl-C when you have enough evidence. It does not stop the process writing the log. grep finds the literal timeout string and reports line numbers rather than interpreting it as a regular expression.

sections.title: Count repeated messages with a clear assumption
sections.body: uniq -c combines adjacent equal lines, so sort first if order does not matter. This simple pipeline counts exact repeated lines; real structured logs often contain a different timestamp per event and need field-aware parsing.
sections.code: grep -F "ERROR" app.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr | head -n 10
sections.walkthrough: The result is a frequency list of identical ERROR lines, not an error rate. With pipefail, an early writer can report a broken pipe when head exits; do not reuse a viewing pipeline as an unquestioned CI pass/fail gate.

takeaway: Use find for paths and grep for text; quote patterns and preserve filenames as arguments. Bounded log inspection and explicit pipeline assumptions are more useful than printing every file.
reviewAnswer: Groups equal lines so adjacent counts are meaningful
question: Why does counting repeated lines usually sort before uniq -c?
wrongAnswers: uniq sorts every input line itself
sort changes error messages into exit codes
hint: uniq compares neighboring lines.
nuance: Do not confuse exact-line counts with rates from timestamped structured logs.

title: Bash passes arguments; quoting defines their boundaries
objective: Read a small build script without splitting paths or accidentally invoking a shell through Go.
introduction: Bash is useful for connecting build and deployment tools on a developer machine. Go itself does not require Bash, Docker or Kubernetes. Learning their boundaries helps when a Go program becomes part of a service workflow; these commands are reading examples, not app terminal commands.

sections.title: Preserve a path as one argument
sections.body: Unquoted parameter expansion can perform word splitting and filename expansion. Quote a variable when its value should be one argument. In Bash, an array preserves several arguments without rebuilding a shell command string.
sections.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -u
project_dir="${1:-.}"
args=(-C "$project_dir" test ./...)
go "${args[@]}"
sections.walkthrough: With a directory containing spaces, the array still supplies one directory argument. The script uses Bash-specific array syntax; it is not a portable /bin/sh script. The -C option changes Go's working directory before running the command.

sections.title: Keep data out of shell syntax
sections.body: When a Go process starts a tool, exec.Command passes an argument vector directly. This avoids asking a shell to reinterpret semicolons, substitutions or spaces. It does not by itself make the target command safe; validate its allowed operation and arguments.
sections.walkthrough: This is native Go code for a development tool. It does not add subprocess execution to the iOS sandbox. Avoid sh -c with concatenated user input.

sections.title: Choose Go when the script stops being glue
sections.body: A few fixed tool invocations can remain a script. Structured retries, complex state, concurrent work and testable domain rules often belong in Go. Quote "$@" when forwarding original arguments, avoid eval, and handle the exit status at the point where failure changes the workflow.

takeaway: Preserve argument boundaries. Use Bash for small orchestration and direct process argument vectors from native Go when no shell language is needed.
reviewAnswer: Preserves each element as one command argument
question: Which statement is correct about quoted bash array expansion?
wrongAnswers: It executes every argument as an independent shell script
It automatically authorizes any path passed by a user
hint: Count arguments after expansion, especially when a path contains spaces.
nuance: Avoiding a shell prevents shell reinterpretation; the invoked tool still needs an allowed-operation contract.

title: Pipelines, exit codes and explicit failure handling
objective: Read pipeline failure behavior and keep configuration and secrets out of command strings.
introduction: A script is another program with success and failure paths. A command printing plausible output can still fail. Pipelines complicate this because the last command can succeed even when an earlier producer failed.

sections.title: Observe the whole pipeline
sections.body: Bash pipefail makes a pipeline fail when a component fails, instead of using only the final command's status. Check that status explicitly at the workflow boundary. set -e has exceptions in conditionals and other constructs, so it is not a replacement for understanding control flow.
sections.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -u -o pipefail
if go test ./... | tee test.log; then
    printf "%s\n" "Tests passed"
else
    printf "%s\n" "Tests failed; inspect test.log" >&2
    exit 1
fi
sections.walkthrough: tee preserves a log while showing output. With pipefail, a failing go test makes the condition fail even when tee succeeds. This script is for a trusted local project and writes one named log file.

sections.title: Pass configuration and inspect one setting
sections.body: A prefix assignment belongs to one child process; export passes a variable to later children from this shell. Check selected non-secret settings instead of dumping the full environment. Already-running services keep their original environment.
sections.code:
APP_ENV=development go run ./cmd/api
export APP_ENV=development
printf "APP_ENV=%s\n" "$APP_ENV"
command -v go
sections.walkthrough: The first line runs a foreground API until you stop it; execute the following commands after it exits or in another shell. The example assumes cmd/api exists and does not require a credential. command -v shows which Go executable Bash will resolve.

sections.title: Make cleanup and retries deliberate
sections.body: A trap can arrange cleanup of resources a script created, but it cannot roll back an external side effect automatically. Avoid rerunning a deployment simply because its status command timed out. Keep a stable operation identifier and inspect the outcome before retrying. As a script grows, move complex state transitions into a program with tests.

takeaway: A successful last pipeline command does not prove upstream success. Preserve exit status, handle failure explicitly, and avoid exposing configuration secrets.
reviewAnswer: Makes upstream failure affect the pipeline status
question: Which statement is correct about bash pipefail?
wrongAnswers: tee reruns every failed Go test automatically
A pipeline always ignores the last command's status
hint: Check which command supplies the pipeline's status before trusting its output.
nuance: set -e has contextual exceptions; an explicit failure branch is often easier to reason about.

title: Processes, signals and exit status
objective: Start one Go service, retain its PID, send TERM and wait for its result.
introduction: A process has a PID, an exit status and open streams. Starting a service in the background does not detach it from responsibility: keep the PID and wait for completion. These commands assume a local Go project with cmd/api and an available port.

sections.title: Start the binary you can stop directly
sections.body: Build first, then run the binary itself in the background. $! is the PID of the latest asynchronous command. A background go run process may introduce a build/launcher process, so it is a poor substitute when practicing exact signal ownership.
sections.code:
mkdir -p bin
go build -o ./bin/api ./cmd/api
./bin/api > api.log 2>&1 &
api_pid=$!
printf "API PID: %s\n" "$api_pid"
sections.walkthrough: Run the launch only after the build succeeds. Both output streams go to api.log. Record this PID instead of searching all processes by a broad application name or terminating unrelated Go jobs.

sections.title: Inspect the process and the listening port
sections.body: ps reports process state; kill -0 checks that a PID can be addressed without sending a signal. lsof is a separately installed utility on some systems and can identify a listening socket; it does not prove the HTTP handler returns useful responses.
sections.code:
ps -p "$api_pid" -o pid,etime,args
kill -0 "$api_pid"
lsof -nP -iTCP:8080 -sTCP:LISTEN
sections.walkthrough: Check that the socket belongs to the binary you launched. If lsof is missing, use your OS socket inspection tool. A process may exit between any two commands; observation is not a lifetime guarantee.

sections.title: Request shutdown and collect the outcome
sections.body: TERM lets a cooperative service drain work. wait observes your shell child and reaps it; an if branch can preserve nonzero status without aborting the shell. SIGKILL prevents application cleanup, so use it only after diagnosing an unresponsive process.
sections.code:
kill -TERM "$api_pid"
if wait "$api_pid"; then
    printf "%s\n" "Service exited successfully"
else
    status=$?
    printf "Service exit status: %s\n" "$status"
fi
tail -n 20 api.log
sections.walkthrough: A graceful service can return zero. A process terminated by a signal may report a nonzero status; inspect its log and shutdown contract. wait works for children of this shell, not any arbitrary PID from another terminal.

takeaway: Keep the child PID, inspect it, request TERM and wait for the outcome. A listening port, a live process and a successful HTTP response are three different observations.
reviewPrompt: Bash wait with a child PID
reviewAnswer: Observes completion and collects the child exit status
question: What does wait "$api_pid" do for a child started in this shell?
wrongAnswers: Kills every process named api
Retries the last failed network request
hint: Background work still has an outcome.
nuance: A PID can be reused after exit; keep ownership instead of targeting processes by vague names.

title: Small scripts: arguments, environment and cleanup
objective: Read required configuration, forward quoted arguments and clean a temporary workspace with a trap.
introduction: A useful script has explicit inputs and predictable cleanup. Bash distinguishes positional arguments, shell variables and exported environment. This lesson puts those pieces into a small test wrapper instead of assuming that adding set -e makes every failure path correct.

sections.title: Read arguments and pass a setting to one process
sections.body: ${1:-.} supplies a default when the first argument is absent or empty. A prefix assignment affects one command environment; export affects later child processes from this shell. Neither changes an already running service.
sections.code:
project_dir="${1:-.}"
printf "Testing: %s\n" "$project_dir"
GOMAXPROCS=2 go -C "$project_dir" test ./...
export APP_ENV=development
printf "APP_ENV=%s\n" "$APP_ENV"
sections.walkthrough: The Go -C flag precedes the test command. The temporary GOMAXPROCS assignment does not permanently change your shell. Never print the complete environment to diagnose one non-secret setting.

sections.title: Validate inputs and clean only owned temporary data
sections.body: The : command with ${name:?message} reports a required input. mktemp creates the workspace, and EXIT runs cleanup on ordinary shell termination. The script forwards "$@" as separate arguments and uses an explicit test branch to preserve failure.
sections.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -u
: "${PROJECT_DIR:?Set PROJECT_DIR to a Go project}"
work_dir=$(mktemp -d) || exit 1
trap 'rm -f "$work_dir/test.log"; rmdir "$work_dir"' EXIT
if go -C "$PROJECT_DIR" test "$@" ./... > "$work_dir/test.log" 2>&1; then
    cat "$work_dir/test.log"
else
    cat "$work_dir/test.log" >&2
    exit 1
fi
sections.walkthrough: Save this as check.sh and call it with bash, PROJECT_DIR set, and optional go test flags such as -count=1. The trap names the one file it owns. SIGKILL and machine failure cannot run shell cleanup.

sections.title: Check syntax before running the script
sections.body: bash -n parses without executing the script; it does not prove that command names, paths or remote systems exist. --help or command -v can establish what is installed. Review changes before making a script executable or putting it into CI.
sections.code:
bash -n check.sh
command -v bash
command -v go
PROJECT_DIR="$PWD" bash check.sh -count=1
sections.walkthrough: Syntax success is silent. The final line runs tests and can download required Go modules; it is an execution step, not another parser check. Keep credentials out of arguments and traces such as bash -x.

takeaway: A script should declare its inputs, preserve argument boundaries and clean only resources it created. Parsing, executing and validating its external effects are separate checks.
reviewAnswer: Passes a variable to subsequently launched child processes
question: What changes when you export APP_ENV?
wrongAnswers: Already running services receive the new value immediately
The value becomes a Kubernetes Secret
hint: A child receives an environment when it starts.
nuance: Configuration is not automatically secret; command traces and logs can reveal it.

title: Git daily work: inspect, branch, stage and commit
objective: Keep working tree, staging area and committed history distinct.
introduction: Git records snapshots, not a magic backup of every unsaved editor buffer. Start in an existing local repository and inspect your changes. The sequence below makes a topic branch, stages one reviewed path and records a local commit; publishing comes in the next lesson.

sections.title: Inspect before selecting a change
sections.body: git status --short summarizes tracked and untracked paths. git diff shows unstaged tracked changes; git diff --staged shows what the next commit contains. Untracked file content is not included in ordinary git diff.
sections.code:
git status --short
git diff -- main.go
git diff --staged
git log -5 --oneline
sections.walkthrough: Compare the two diff views. A file can have both staged and unstaged edits, and the next commit includes only the staged snapshot. -- separates options/revisions from the path main.go.

sections.title: Put a reviewed change on a topic branch
sections.body: switch -c creates and selects a new branch at the current commit. add stages the named content. Inspect the staged result before committing, rather than using add . when a repository includes unrelated experiments or local credentials.
sections.code:
git switch -c feature/health-check
git add -- main.go
git diff --staged
git commit -m "Add health endpoint"
sections.walkthrough: Use an unused branch name and a real main.go change. The commit remains local until you push it. If a hook fails, inspect its output and rerun the necessary check rather than bypassing it automatically.

sections.title: Unstage without discarding your edit
sections.body: restore --staged changes the index back toward HEAD while leaving the working file intact. A plain restore of the working tree has a different, destructive meaning. Check both views after unstaging to make the distinction visible.
sections.code:
git restore --staged -- main.go
git status --short
git diff -- main.go
sections.walkthrough: Use this on a staged change before committing. Your edits should now be unstaged. This is not a command to undo an existing commit; history repair and reverting a published change are different operations.

takeaway: Review unstaged and staged diffs separately, stage intended paths and commit on a named branch. Unstaging an edit preserves it; overwriting the working tree may discard it.
reviewAnswer: Shows the snapshot changes queued for the next commit
question: Which changes does git diff --staged show?
wrongAnswers: Only untracked files not yet added
Every commit already pushed to every remote
hint: The staging area is the next snapshot.
nuance: git restore --staged preserves the working file; plain git restore can replace it.

title: Git collaboration: fetch, compare, stash and push
objective: Inspect upstream changes before integration and keep unfinished work recoverable.
introduction: A remote-tracking branch is your local record of a remote branch at the last fetch. Fetching updates that record without integrating it into your current branch. The examples assume an origin remote, a main branch and an existing topic branch you own.

sections.title: Fetch and compare before merging
sections.body: remote -v shows fetch and push destinations; inspect those before publishing. fetch origin updates remote-tracking references. The three-dot diff compares the topic branch against its merge base with origin/main, highlighting the branch contribution.
sections.code:
git remote -v
git fetch origin
git log --oneline HEAD..origin/main
git diff origin/main...HEAD
sections.walkthrough: HEAD..origin/main lists commits reachable from origin/main but not HEAD. Fetch does not change your working files. A remote URL may contain sensitive information; avoid pasting it indiscriminately into public logs.

sections.title: Temporarily store an unfinished tracked change
sections.body: stash push -u includes untracked files as well as tracked edits, but not ignored files by default. apply restores a stash while retaining its saved entry. Inspect and resolve any conflicts before deciding to drop the saved copy.
sections.code:
git stash push -u -m "WIP before syncing"
git stash list
git stash show --stat "stash@{0}"
git stash apply "stash@{0}"
git status --short
sections.walkthrough: Only apply when a stash entry actually exists. apply can conflict; it does not mean every file was restored cleanly. The retained stash is useful until the restored work is checked. A stash is local, not a shared backup.

sections.title: Integrate deliberately and publish the branch
sections.body: On a clean main branch, pull --ff-only refuses an implicit merge when histories diverge. A topic branch push sets its upstream without rewriting remote history. A rejected push is evidence to fetch and inspect, not a reason to force-push blindly.
sections.code:
git switch main
git pull --ff-only origin main
git switch feature/health-check
git push -u origin feature/health-check
sections.walkthrough: Resolve or save local changes before switching branches. The pull updates main only if fast-forward is possible. Pushing the topic branch publishes commits; it does not merge them into main or submit an application release.

takeaway: Fetch and compare before integrating. Preserve unfinished work, inspect conflicts and push the intended branch. Fast-forward refusal is a useful signal that history needs a deliberate decision.
reviewAnswer: Updates remote-tracking refs without merging into HEAD
question: What does git fetch origin normally update?
wrongAnswers: It merges origin/main into every local branch
It publishes all uncommitted files
hint: Fetch and integration are separate operations.
nuance: A rejected push should lead to comparison, not an automatic forced history rewrite.

title: Go toolbelt: modules, tests, vet and build
objective: Use the native Go CLI to inspect a module and check a service before packaging it.
introduction: A useful Go development loop checks the module boundary, formatting, tests, static diagnostics and the final build. These commands are for the native Go toolchain on a development machine; platform support and build tags can change which packages are selected.

sections.title: Locate the module and inspect dependencies
sections.body: go version identifies the toolchain. go env GOMOD GOWORK prints selected module/workspace files without dumping every environment setting. list -m all describes the selected build list; mod why explains why a dependency is needed.
sections.code:
go version
go env GOMOD GOWORK
go list -m all
go mod why -m golang.org/x/sync
sections.walkthrough: Run inside your module; the selected module file should be the one you expect. The last dependency is an example: if it is not required, Go explains that. Module commands may access the configured proxy and network.

sections.title: Format, test and inspect suspicious code
sections.body: gofmt -l lists formatting differences without rewriting files. test checks packages; -race adds supported native race instrumentation. vet reports suspicious constructs rather than proving semantic correctness. A clean run still depends on meaningful tests.
sections.code:
gofmt -l .
go test ./...
go test -race ./...
go vet ./...
